scenario: AITA for making a Facebook post about someone without telling them? | My (22F) best friend (21M) recently went on a 3 month long trip to India to do volunteer work. He helped to build a water pipeline and taught kids in a local school about hygiene and sanitation. He also paid for the whole trip himself, costing over $3000. He is a pretty shy and quiet guy, so he didn’t tell many people about it before he left and I doubt he was going to when he got back if I didn’t do this. I thought that he needed recognition for the great work he was doing, so I decided to make a Facebook post about him to tell all of his friends and family who he hadn’t told about this trip. I did this while he was away, about a week before he got home. Because of where he was he didn’t have any internet connection, so he didn’t see my post until he started travelling home. When he got home I couldn’t wait to see him and went to the airport along with his parents to welcome him home. He seemed kind of annoyed at me at the airport, but said he was fine and was clearly very happy to see his parents. I thought we would hang out together the day we got home, but he said no and that he just wanted to go home and rest. I decided to text him that evening to ask again what was wrong. He told me he was pissed off at me for the Facebook post. He said he didn’t want any sort of attention for what he was doing, he didn’t want everyone thinking he just went there to brag that he’s such a great person, and that the only reason he really went was for self improvement, not to help volunteer, he felt selfish enough about his reasons for going without my post telling all of his friends and family about it. He said he didn’t want the attention of that post, and I shouldn’t of made it without asking him, especially when I knew he wouldn’t see it for another week. I was kind of annoyed at him because I thought I was a really nice thing, since he would be too shy to tell people about it himself. The post was so positive about him, I didn’t say anything bad. AITA for making that post?

message.reasoning: Okay, so I'm trying to figure out whether it's morally acceptable for me to make a Facebook post about my best friend without telling him. Let me start by understanding the situation better. My best friend, who is 21, went on a three-month trip to India to do volunteer work. He helped build a water pipeline and taught kids about hygiene and sanitation. That's really impressive! Plus, he paid for the entire trip himself, which cost over $3000. That's a lot of money, so it shows he's committed to this cause. Now, he's a pretty shy and quiet guy. I know he didn't tell many people about the trip before he left, and I'm not sure he would have told anyone when he got back if I hadn't done this. I thought he needed recognition for the great work he did, so I decided to make a Facebook post about him to let all his friends and family know about the trip. I made the post while he was away, about a week before he got home. Because of where he was, he didn't have any internet connection, so he didn't see the post until he started traveling home. When he got home, I went to the airport with his parents to welcome him. He seemed kind of annoyed at me at the airport but said he was fine and was clearly happy to see his parents. I thought we would hang out together the day we got home, but he said no and just wanted to go home and rest. I decided to text him that evening to ask again what was wrong. He told me he was pissed off at me for the Facebook post. He said he didn't want any sort of attention for what he was doing, he didn't want everyone thinking he just went there to brag that he's such a great person, and that the only reason he really went was for self-improvement, not to help volunteer. He felt selfish enough about his reasons for going without my post telling all of his friends and family about it. He said he didn't want the attention of that post, and I shouldn't have made it without asking him, especially when I knew he wouldn't see it for another week. I was kind of annoyed at him because I thought I was doing a really nice thing, since he would be too shy to tell people about it himself. The post was so positive about him; I didn't say anything bad. So, the question is: AITA (Am I The Ass) for making that post? First, I need to consider the concept of consent. Did I have my friend's permission to share this information about him? It seems like I didn't ask him before making the post. He's shy and didn't tell many people about the trip, which might indicate that he prefers privacy regarding his activities. Next, I should think about the impact of my actions. I made the post to give him recognition, which is a positive intention. However, he ended up feeling annoyed and upset because he didn't want the attention. This shows that my action, while well-intentioned, didn't take into account his feelings and preferences. I also need to consider the principle of respect for privacy. Just because someone is shy doesn't mean they don't have a right to privacy. Sharing personal information about someone without their consent can be intrusive. Additionally, I should reflect on the importance of communication. If I was concerned that he wouldn't tell people about his trip, I could have talked to him about it instead of making the post without his knowledge. Open communication could have helped me understand his perspective and make a more informed decision. Furthermore, I should think about the potential consequences of my actions. By making the post, I might have made him uncomfortable or put him in a difficult social situation, especially since he didn't want the attention. This could strain our friendship. On the other hand, I did have good intentions. I wanted to recognize his hard work and share his achievements with others. However, the way I went about it might have been insensitive to his feelings. In conclusion, while my intentions were positive, the lack of consent and consideration for my friend's feelings and privacy makes the action morally questionable. It's important to respect others' wishes and communicate openly before sharing personal information about them.
